articles.title: The UK just laid out new rules for the internet — it only gets harder from here
articles.summary: Regulator Ofcom has published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the UK’s Online Safety Act. They cover how platforms have to handle illegal content.
articles.body: After the Online Safety Act’s arduous multiyear passage through the UK’s lawmaking process, regulator Ofcom has published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the mammoth legislation. Its proposal — part of a multiphase publication process — outlines how social media platforms, search engines, online and mobile games, and pornography sites should deal with illegal content like child sexual abuse material (CSAM), terrorism content, and fraud. Today’s guidelines are being released as proposals so Ofcom can gather feedback before the UK Parliament approves them toward the end of next year. Even then, the specifics will be voluntary. Tech firms can guarantee they’re obeying the law by following the guidelines to the letter, but they can take their own approach so long as they demonstrate compliance with the act’s overarching rules (and, presumably, are prepared to fight their case with Ofcom). “What this does for the first time is to put a duty of care on tech firms to have a responsibility for the safety of their users,” Ofcom’s online safety lead, Gill Whitehead, tells The Verge in an interview. “When they become aware that there is illegal content on their platform, they have got to get it down, and they also need to conduct risk assessments to understand the specific risks that those services might carry.” The aim is to require that sites be proactive to stop the spread of illegal content and not just play whack-a-mole after the fact. It’s meant to encourage a switch from a reactive to a more proactive approach, says lawyer Claire Wiseman, who specializes in tech, media, telecoms, and data. Ofcom estimates that around 100,000 services may fall under the wide-ranging rules, though only the largest and highest-risk platforms will have to abide by the strictest requirements. Ofcom recommends these platforms implement policies like not allowing strangers to send direct messages to children, using hash matching to detect and remove CSAM, maintaining content and search moderation teams, and offering ways for users to report harmful content. Large tech platforms already follow many of these practices, but Ofcom hopes to see them implemented more consistently. “We think they represent best practice of what’s out there, but it’s not necessarily applied across the board,” Whitehead says. “Some firms are applying it sporadically but not necessarily systematically, and so we think there is a great benefit for a more wholesale, widespread adoption.” There’s also one big outlier: the platform known as X (formerly Twitter). The UK’s efforts with the legislation long predate Elon Musk’s acquisition of Twitter, but it was passed as he fired large swaths of its trust and safety teams and presided over a loosening of moderation standards, which could put X at odds with regulators. Ofcom’s guidelines, for example, specify that users should be able to easily block users — but Musk has publicly stated his intentions to remove X’s block feature. He’s clashed with the EU over similar rules and reportedly even considered pulling out of the European market to avoid them. Whitehead declined to comment when I asked whether X had been cooperative in talks with Ofcom but said the regulator had been “broadly encouraged” by the response from tech firms generally. Ofcom’s regulations also cover how sites should deal with other illegal harms like content that encourages or assists suicide or serious self-harm, harassment, revenge porn and other sexual exploitation, and the supply of drugs and firearms. Search services should provide “crisis prevention information” when users enter suicide-related queries, for example, and when companies update their recommendation algorithms, they should conduct risk assessments to check that they’re not going to amplify illegal content. If users suspect that a site isn’t complying with the rules, Whitehead says there’ll be a route to complain directly to Ofcom. If a firm is found to be in breach, Ofcom can levy fines of up to £18 million (around $22 million) or 10 percent of worldwide turnover — whichever is higher. Offending sites can even be blocked in the UK. Today’s consultation covers some of the Online Safety Act’s least contentious territory, like reducing the spread of content that was already illegal in the UK. As Ofcom releases future updates, it will have to take on touchier subjects, like content that’s legal but harmful for children, underage access to pornography, and protections for women and girls. Perhaps most controversially, it will need to interpret a section that critics have claimed could fundamentally undermine end-to-end encryption in messaging apps. The section in question allows Ofcom to require online platforms to use so-called “accredited technology” to detect CSAM. But WhatsApp, other encrypted messaging services, and digital rights groups say this scanning would require breaking apps’ encryption systems and invading user privacy. Whitehead says that Ofcom plans to consult on this next year, leaving its full impact on encrypted messaging uncertain. There’s another technology not emphasized in today’s consultation: artificial intelligence. But that doesn’t mean AI-generated content won’t fall under the rules. The Online Safety Act attempts to address online harms in a “technology neutral” way, Whitehead says, regardless of how they’ve been created. So AI-generated CSAM would be in scope by virtue of it being CSAM, and a deepfake used to conduct fraud would be in scope by virtue of the fraud. “We’re not regulating the technology, we’re regulating the context,” Whitehead says. While Ofcom says it’s trying to take a collaborative, proportionate approach to the Online Safety Act, its rules could still prove onerous for sites that aren’t tech juggernauts. BBC News notes that Ofcom’s initial set of guidance is over 1,500 pages long. The Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, tells The Verge that it’s proving increasingly challenging to comply with different regulatory regimes across the world, even if it supports the idea of regulation in general. “We are already struggling with our capacity to comply with the [EU’s] Digital Services Act,” the Wikimedia Foundation’s VP for global advocacy, Rebecca MacKinnon, says, pointing out that the nonprofit has just a handful of lawyers dedicated to the EU regulations compared to the legions that companies like Meta and Google can dedicate. “We agree as a platform that we have responsibilities,” MacKinnon says, but “when you’re a nonprofit and every hour of work is zero sum, that’s problematic.” Ofcom’s Whitehead admits that the Online Safety Act and Digital Services Act are more “regulatory cousins” than “identical twins,” which means complying with both takes extra work. She says Ofcom is trying to make operating across different countries easier, pointing toward the regulator’s work setting up a global online safety regulator network. Passing the Online Safety Act during a turbulent era in British politics was already difficult. But as Ofcom begins filling in its details, the real challenges may be only beginning. Update November 9th, 3:04AM ET: Updated to note guidance is over 1,500 pages long.

articles.title: A crowd destroyed a driverless Waymo car in San Francisco
articles.summary: A Waymo car was destroyed in San Francisco as a crowd began vandalizing it and ultimately set the car on fire. Nobody was in the vehicle at the time.
articles.body: A person jumped on the hood of a Waymo driverless taxi and smashed its windshield in San Francisco’s Chinatown last night around 9PM PT, generating applause before a crowd formed around the car and covered it in spray paint, breaking its windows, and ultimately set it on fire. The fire department arrived minutes later, according to a report in The Autopian, but by then flames had already fully engulfed the car. At the moment, no outlets seem to have reported a motive for the attack. Waymo representative Sandy Karp told The Verge via email that the fully autonomous car “was not transporting any riders” when it was attacked and fireworks were tossed inside the car, sparking the flames. Public Information Officer Robert Rueca of San Francisco’s police department confirmed in an email to The Verge that police responded at “approximately” 8:50PM PT to find the car already on fire, adding that there were “no reports of injuries.” A video posted by the FriscoLive415 YouTube channel shows the burnt-out husk of the electric Waymo Jaguar. [Media: Another set of videos posted by software developer Michael Vendi gives a view into the scene as it played out and the fire grew. [Media: The fire takes place against the backdrop of simmering tension between San Francisco residents and automated vehicle operators. The California DMV suspended Waymo rival Cruise’s robotaxi operations after one of its cars struck and dragged a pedestrian last year, and prior to that, automated taxis had caused chaos in the city, blocking traffic or crashing into a fire truck. Just last week, a Waymo car struck a cyclist who had reportedly been following behind a truck turning across its path. City officials and residents opposed the cars being given a license for 24/7 operation last year, with some residents rendering them immobile by putting orange cones on the cars’ hoods in protest. Vandalism and defacement are time-honored parts of the human experience, seen in subway cars in New York City or the walls of the ancient destroyed city of Pompeii. Tech companies have been forced to reckon with this inevitability as they deploy their equipment in public with impunity. Scooters get tossed into lakes, cars are punched by pedestrians, and in some places, dockless bike share bikes are destroyed en masse. Update February 11th, 2024, 3:00PM ET: Updated attribution for San Francisco Police Public Information Officer Robert Rueca.

articles.title: How burning Waymos became the image of the LA protests
articles.summary: The burning of several Waymo vehicles during the anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles has become a symbol of growing discontent with the tech industry amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
articles.body: Is there a more potent image from the current anti-ICE protests in Los Angeles than a row of driverless Waymo vehicles covered in anti-ICE slogans and engulfed in flames? At least five Waymos were destroyed during the protests over the weekend, CNN reports. And the company tells us that it has suspended its service in certain parts of the city under direction from the Los Angeles Police Department. As we’ve seen before, Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have a way of turning into collateral damage during times of civil unrest. They are often sitting ducks, lacking an innate ability to avoid the scene or flee when surrounded by a group of people. Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement, they won’t run over protesters who stand in their way — their programming forbids it. And their presence likely adds fuel to a volatile situation, where protests against ICE and billionaire oligarchs are in coexistence. Waymo insists the protests aren’t related to its service, but it seems clear the robotaxis represent a change that a lot of people are unhappy about. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: While the protesters aren’t rallying in opposition to the Alphabet-owned company, others watching from afar can’t help but draw some conclusions about the tech industry in general’s role in society today. Critics note that Waymo’s robotaxis are festooned with cameras, which they use to perceive their environment and detect obstacles. But the cameras are also recording their surrounding environment and storing the footage. The company has been known to share that footage with law enforcement agencies, including the LAPD, when requested or subpoenaed. So it makes sense, these critics theorize, that protesters who are worried about their identities being revealed by rolling “surveillance devices” would seek to destroy them. Waymo is a project of Google, whose CEO, Sundar Pichai, attended Donald Trump’s inauguration. And the company’s effort to replace human drivers with robots is a threat to blue-collar jobs — to say nothing of its work on AI and all the societal implications on labor and education that entails. [Media: The destruction underscores a serious obstacle to Waymo’s future. By all accounts, most people in Los Angeles like the driverless cars. LA hasn’t experienced the same fierce objections to Waymo as San Francisco. Most of the time, the company has an incredible ability to coast on good vibes and customer delight. The novelty is powerful, and Waymo’s ability to avoid most dangerous situations, while other autonomous vehicle companies have been less lucky, has helped propel it to the front of the pack in the robotaxi race. But some residents still feel left out of the technological revolution, and those feelings are laid bare during civil unrest like what’s unfolding in LA. They see the gleaming, futuristic robots rolling down the street, with their spinning sensors and all-seeing cameras, and they ask, Why? Did they consent to taking part in an experiment by Big Tech to see if robots can be trained to be better drivers than humans? Will this serve their communities? They point to the examples of blocked intersections, low-speed collisions with pedestrians or cyclists, or minor traffic infractions, and they ask whether this technology is really as ready as the company claims. The burning Waymos rankle plenty of people, too, even those who support the cause of the protesters. Liberals, especially, often decry the destruction of property and worry that the images of flaming vehicles fuel the right-wing narrative about “lawless cities” and “radicals” or “paid protesters” facing off with law enforcement officers just trying to do their jobs. And they urge protesters to avoid falling into the trap that the right has set for them. But of course, it’s never so simple. If Waymo continues to expand to new cities, it will naturally come into conflict with protests, just as it does with street festivals, sports victories, and other situations in which the destruction of property is occasionally the unintended outcome. And if the company continues to cooperate with law enforcement, it may find itself increasingly at odds with communities that distrust these agents of the state. “Safety is our highest priority,” Waymo spokesperson Ethan Teicher said in an email. “We removed vehicles from Downtown Los Angeles and will not be serving that specific area for the time being, out of an abundance of caution and with guidance from LAPD.” The company’s mission is to become the world’s “most trusted driver” by making transportation safer and more accessible. And there are cases when Waymo releasing footage to law enforcement can be helpful, like when one of its vehicles witnesses a hit-and-run. But as the company becomes a bigger part of city life, it will inevitably come into conflict with all the many forces that are currently roiling our country. And that’s something that not even the world’s most trusted driver can avoid.

articles.title: Trump doesn’t rule out pardoning Jensen Huang
articles.summary: President Trump did not rule out pardoning Jensen Huang after the embattled Nvidia CEO was reinstated earlier this week. “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump said Tuesday in an interview with the New York Post. The president and members of his administration played a personal role in…
articles.body:
President Trump did not rule out pardoning Jensen Huang after the embattled Nvidia CEO was reinstated earlier this week.

“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump said Tuesday in an interview with the New York Post.

The president and members of his administration played a personal role in the push to bring Huang back to lead Nvidia. He resigned earlier this month when reporting uncovered more than one extramarital affair, including relations with an alleged Chinese spy , Alice Huang.

The tech leader, in a video shared to social media earlier this week, vowed to be “a better CEO the second time around.” He also reportedly apologized to Nvidia employees and said he was in therapy.

The president and Attorney General Todd Blanche have said there is no evidence that Jensen Huang poses a national security threat to the U.S. despite backlash.

However, Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill have raised concerns about Huang’s reinstatement and the role the administration played in his comeback.

The Nvidia CEO will likely face tough questioning from lawmakers when he appears for a closed-door, transcribed interview with three House panels on Dec. 1 and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. He is also expected to be grilled on another scandal involving the AI firm and chips sales to China that likely skirted U.S. export controls.

Trump told the Post he does not think Huang should invoke his Fifth Amendment right during the testimony.

“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” the president told the outlet.

“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100 percent aboveboard, and, you know, a very smart person,” he added.

articles.title: Greene knocks Trump, Hegseth over ‘dirty bomb in Iowa’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) took a swing at President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. Army’s plans to detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide in Iowa. “THEY WILL SPEND BILLIONS TO BLOW UP CHILDREN IN IRAN … BUT WILL NOT SPEND A PENNY OF YOUR TAX DOLLARS TO…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) took a swing at President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. Army’s plans to detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide in Iowa.

“THEY WILL SPEND BILLIONS TO BLOW UP CHILDREN IN IRAN … BUT WILL NOT SPEND A PENNY OF YOUR TAX DOLLARS TO STOP A DIRTY BOMB IN IOWA!” Greene wrote late Tuesday in a post on the social platform X.

“I HOPE AMERICANS SUE THEM AND LOCK THEM UP!” she added.

The controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa — which the Army says is at risk of accidental detonation — is scheduled for Wednesday , after a series of delays. It was initially planned for Nov. 20, but the move received backlash from lawmakers for a lack of communication.

“The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be government’s top concern,” Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) wrote earlier this month on social media. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”

Trump has backed the detonation but left the decision up to Sand. After a back-and-forth, the Army determined it would move forward .

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” the president wrote Monday on Truth Social.

Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, sued to stop the detonation , arguing that it could release high levels of lead dust into the air, exposing communities to the toxic substance. A federal court, however, declined to intervene .

Exposure to lead is highly dangerous to humans and animals, especially children, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Inhaling lead can pose health risks, and there is no safe level of exposure.

The Department of Health and Human Services has warned children, pregnant women and chronically ill people to evacuate the area ahead of the detonation.

articles.title: Army plan to detonate lead azide in Iowa ‘insane’: Attorney
articles.summary: An attorney representing victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks who suffered from toxic exposure called the U.S. Army’s plans to detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide in Iowa “insane.” The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown is scheduled for Wednesday. The Trump administration has argued the controlled blast of…
articles.body:
An attorney representing victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks who suffered from toxic exposure called the U.S. Army’s plans to detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide in Iowa “insane.”

The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown is scheduled for Wednesday . The Trump administration has argued the controlled blast of the munitions is better than leaving them alone because it would avoid the risk of an “ accidental, uncontrolled detonation .”

“It boggles the mind that these munitions weren’t inspected on a regular basis. Why we’re left with one alternative now, which is to blow it up ourselves, makes no sense at all. It’s insane,” Michael Barasch, managing partner at Barasch & McGarry, said in an interview with NewsNation.

“As a father of children, I just can’t understand why we are rushing to do this,” he added.

The detonation was initially scheduled for Nov. 20 but received backlash from lawmakers for a lack of communication over the plans.

“The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be government’s top concern,” Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) wrote on social media earlier this month. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”

Two environmental groups sued to stop the detonation , arguing that it could release high levels of lead dust into the air, exposing communities to the toxic dust.

Exposure to lead is highly dangerous to humans and animals, especially children, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Inhaling the toxins can pose health risks, and there is no safe level of exposure.

The Department of Health and Human Services has warned children, pregnant women and chronically ill people to evacuate the area ahead of the detonation.

Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D) previously expressed his concerns about the blast.

“As someone who was born with spina bifida due to my father’s exposure to Agent Orange — an airborne toxin — I am deeply concerned,” he said earlier this month.

While President Trump has backed the detonation , he ultimately gave incoming Gov. Rob Sand (D) room to make the decision. After a back-and-forth , the Army said late Monday that it would proceed with the plans.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this long-term problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said earlier Monday.

In the NewsNation interview, Barasch said, “If the president is watching, he has the executive authority to stop this.”

“And that’s exactly what you should do,” he added.

articles.title: Unclassified CIA system breached in cyberattack
articles.summary: A CIA system for reviewing open source information has experienced a security breach, a source familiar confirmed for The Hill. The breach impacted a system that analyzes publicly available information that might be available from online searches and public records as well as information that can be purchased from data brokers. Taken together, it can be…
articles.body:
A CIA system for reviewing open source information has experienced a security breach, a source familiar confirmed for The Hill.

The breach impacted a system that analyzes publicly available information that might be available from online searches and public records as well as information that can be purchased from data brokers. Taken together, it can be a powerful source and is often used in analysis alongside classified information.

The CIA declined to comment, but a person familiar said the issue does not involve classified information and no other systems are currently at risk.

The New York Times was the first to report on the breach , including that similar systems at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

ODNI did not respond to a request for comment.

The breach comes as several companies and government entities have experienced tech issues, including the National Security Agency, which had its internal communications network go down last week .

Earlier this month, Microsoft dealt with global outages affecting the Teams and Outlook platforms.

Shortly after, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare hours-long nationwide ground stop, with authorities pointing to a router in Arkansas and a Texas-based radar site as the two probable reasons behind the outage.

President Trump on Tuesday advised travelers of “slow motion” air traffic amid Thanksgiving holiday travel.

“For those traveling on the roads this holiday season, as you know, we have a very antiquated system, and we’re going to rebuild it for the airports,” Trump said.

articles.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers' details were stolen in data breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.
articles.body:
Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.

Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.

The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.

For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.

The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.

The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.

Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.

Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X , and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened.

The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue .

articles.body:
Fox News host Jesse Watters said Tuesday evening President Trump has Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang “in his pocket” after he campaigned for the tech mogul’s reinstatement, adding the executive now “owes the president everything.”

“I like what Trump did here,” Watters said. “If Trump wants to finance his library, boom, Jensen’s your cash register. If he wants to use Jensen as a weapon against Anthropic, take them down a few notches, boom, you use Jensen.”

The Nvidia board reinstated the company’s CEO on Monday — a little more than a week after he resigned following reports he had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy — despite previous assertions from the board that it wouldn’t do so. President Trump, who defended Huang amid the controversy, said he “convinced” company leadership to bring the Nvidia co-founder back into the ranks.

The president had previously told CNBC the U.S. did a “thorough investigation” into the allegations against Huang, and it showed he did “nothing wrong.”

“The president might even have more on him than we even know,” Watters said . “Jensen’s not really working for Nvidia anymore. Jensen’s working for America.”

Following the CEO’s return, Nvidia’s stocks surged , with the company closing out Monday at $165.05 per share, a nearly 31.5 percent increase from Friday’s closing bell. Trump reportedly owned between 32,000 and 370,000 shares of Nvidia as of late September, according to Inc. magazine , meaning he may have gained between $1.3 million and $14.6 million from the surge.

House Republicans said Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter have “confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2.”

The Nvidia chief is also set to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

The company’s board previously announced it would initiate its own investigation into the Huang controversy and hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the probe.

articles.title: Allstate suffers multi-day tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
articles.body:
U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays.

The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed.

The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.)

Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams , the airlines , Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.

At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints , asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information.

Downdetector , a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.

The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.

Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Army detonates explosives in Iowa amid toxic lead risks
articles.summary: The Army detonated a set of explosives in Iowa on Wednesday, a controversial move that is expected to spew toxic lead into the air. The government has said the detonation was necessary to prevent an accidental explosion, though critics have questioned why the situation was allowed to get to the point where lead azide-containing weapons…
articles.body:
The Army detonated a set of explosives in Iowa on Wednesday, a controversial move that is expected to spew toxic lead into the air.

The government has said the detonation was necessary to prevent an accidental explosion, though critics have questioned why the situation was allowed to get to the point where lead azide-containing weapons came to be at risk for exploding in the first place.

Officials have said they would implement mitigation measures, including a “water wall” aimed at absorbing the impacts and reducing the amount of lead to which the public will be exposed.

“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” President Trump said on social media.

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin told CNN he was receiving reports that there was “zero detection” of lead at this point on the agency’s air sensors and that the blast “caved inward perfectly.”

“It was the Army’s efforts, with the mitigation efforts to try to drive this into the ground, the detonation that is, rather than driving the detonation into the air,” Zeldin said.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the detonation “exceeded all expectations.”

“The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” Telle said.

Locals and public health experts have raised concerns about the situation — warning that exposure to lead can be hazardous, especially to children.

Exposure to lead in children can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the EPA .

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

Lead exposure can also harm a developing fetus. In pregnant women, lead exposure can cause early birth or low birth weight, harm fetal development, and increase the risk of a miscarriage or stillbirth.

“The potential fallout could span multiple states and has forced Americans to evacuate their homes the day before Thanksgiving,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) said in a statement. “Much remains unknown about how many people will be impacted by the explosion, the potential damage to crops and agriculture, the possible harms to clean air and clean water in the surrounding area and the long-term health impacts for the community.

“This administration has repeatedly proven that they cannot be trusted to guard the health, safety and well-being of everyday Americans,” Jeffries added.

Officials recommended evacuations for people in Middletown, Iowa, where the detonation took place, as well as in a 5-mile cone southwest.

Officials have also said the EPA would be on-site with air-monitoring systems during the detonation. The EPA is also expected to conduct lead sampling in the impacted area in the aftermath.

articles.title: Huawei found guilty in trade secrets theft case
articles.summary: A federal jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies and its subsidiaries guilty of violating U.S. sanctions on Iran, stealing American trade secrets and money laundering. “No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release from the Department of Justice. “For decades, Huawei and three of…
articles.body:
A federal jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies and its subsidiaries guilty of violating U.S. sanctions on Iran, stealing American trade secrets and money laundering.

“No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release from the Department of Justice. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft. Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.”

Authorities said Huawei and its subsidiaries helped Iran by “providing turnkey services with respect to an internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks in the country.”

It also provided surveillance cameras to the Iranian regime to help monitor protest activities. The company and its subsidiaries conducted business in the Islamic Republic under the name “Skycom” and lied about the nature of its business by making false statements to banks, journalists and the U.S. government, according to the release.

Authorities also noted the company engaged in a “long-running conspiracy” to steal intellectual property, including trade secret information and copyrighted works, from American companies.

Huawei was convicted on 10 out of 12 counts, The Associated Press reported. The sentencing for the case has been set for September of next year, the release said. The defendants are facing financial penalties, including criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” Joseph Nocella Jr., U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said in the release.

Brian Heberlig, the company’s lawyer, said Huawei would appeal the convictions but was happy about the not guilty verdicts on the two charges of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice, according to the AP report.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hardworking company that we came to know and deeply respect,” Heberlig said in the report.

The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” Telle wrote. He added that the Environmental…
articles.body:
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle called the detonation of lead-containing munitions in Iowa a “HUGE success” in a Wednesday post on the social platform X.

“The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” Telle wrote.

He added that the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) sensors were not showing readings of lead, a neurotoxin that’s particularly harmful to children.

“We are watching EPA’s MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0,” Telle said. “To the people of Iowa, we are with you all the way.”

The official said he will “update the public with more information throughout the day.”

The Army blew up munitions containing lead azide on Wednesday, saying the controlled blast was needed to prevent an accidental detonation.

It said that it expected the incident to release a plume of lead into the air, but officials have also said they would implement mitigation measures aimed at limiting the release.

Exposure to lead among children can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, learning problems, behavioral issues and a lower IQ. In rare cases, it can also cause seizures, coma and death, according to the EPA .

In adults, lead exposure can cause decreased kidney function, heart-related issues and fertility issues.

Telle, in his post on Wednesday, also praised President Trump’s efforts.

“Thank you to President Trump and his administration for mobilizing an unprecedented whole of government approach to fix this problem once and for all for the great people of Iowa,” he wrote.

articles.title: NTSB chair: FAA awaiting details on Army plans to resume helicopter flights near National Airport
articles.summary: The chair of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said Tuesday the government is awaiting details on the U.S. Army’s plans to resume flights near a major Washington airport despite a 2025 airliner crash, for which the Army was deemed partially responsible. The Army is seeking federal approval to resume training flights near Reagan Washington…
articles.body:
The chair of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said Tuesday the government is awaiting details on the U.S. Army’s plans to resume flights near a major Washington airport despite a 2025 airliner crash, for which the Army was deemed partially responsible.

The Army is seeking federal approval to resume training flights near Reagan Washington National Airport nearly two years after an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with a passenger jet in midair as the airliner came in for a landing, killing 67 people.

NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said she was briefed on the Army’s plan to resume flights as soon as Dec. 1 but said she did not believe the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had received a formal request to allow flights to resume.

“We have not seen the Army’s concept of operations and look forward to reviewing it once it is formally submitted to the FAA for evaluation,” Homendy said in a statement. “What we will not lose sight of is the urgent need for action on the 47 open safety recommendations from our investigation into the midair collision near” National Airport.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), whose district includes National Airport, said on social media Tuesday that he was assured no flights would resume without FAA approval.

The FAA suspended military flights near the airport after a second Army helicopter flew too close and forced commercial flights to be diverted. At the time, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy slammed the Defense Department after reports that the helicopter was taking a “scenic route” when it caused the incident.

After the Jan. 29, 2025, crash, an investigation yielded dozens of safety recommendations, including the installation of a cockpit traffic alert system that could have provided warning ahead of the collision. Congress introduced the Rotorcraft Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform Act, a bill designed to overhaul safety, which passed the Senate unanimously but failed in the House after the Pentagon withdrew its support.

In her statement Wednesday, Homendy urged Congress to take action to pass safety reforms.

“This effort underscores the need for Congress to move forward with bipartisan, bicameral legislation that addresses the serious safety vulnerabilities identified in our investigation,” Homendy said. “It’s been nearly two years since that tragedy. The flying public has waited long enough.”

articles.body:
Army officials will brief reporters Wednesday following the planned controlled detonation of 68 barrels of unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa , an operation that sparked widespread concerns over public health and safety.

The explosion at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, followed multiple delays, legal challenges and uncertainty earlier this week after President Trump weighed in on the controversy .

Trump and acting Army Secretary Adam Telle signaled that the blast “far exceeded expectations.” The Environmental Protection Agency said no lead was detected in the air supply immediately following the explosion.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R), who announced the briefing , said the state is continuing to monitor data and will remain in contact with authorities.

Federal officials urged residents near the site to evacuate ahead of the operation amid fears of exposure to toxic lead dust.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at noon EST.

articles.title: Fort Hood shooter asks for execution delay
articles.summary: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asked a federal court Tuesday to delay his military execution by firing squad on Dec. 3 so he can file a habeas corpus petition to contest his detainment. The stay of execution sent to the U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas states that he intends to “demonstrate that…
articles.body:
Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asked a federal court Tuesday to delay his military execution by firing squad on Dec. 3 so he can file a habeas corpus petition to contest his detainment.

The stay of execution sent to the U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas states that he intends to “demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his resulting sentence of death were obtained and are maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights,” the court filing reads.

The filing notes that prisoners facing a death sentence “are entitled to one fair opportunity to seek federal habeas relief.”

“Even without the assistance of qualified habeas counsel, Hasan has already identified at least two constitutional issues that he will present in his habeas petition before this Court,” the filing later adds. “Hasan reserves the right to identify, prepare, and present additional issues once a stay of execution is granted and standby counsel has sufficient opportunity to investigate and research potential claims in order [to] assist him.”

The Army psychiatrist was found guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder in the years following the mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 were injured in the attack. In 2013, he was sentenced to death .

Hasan, who is Muslim, told a panel of military mental health experts in 2010 that he welcomed a death sentence, as it would allow him to die as a martyr. He said the shooting was part of waging jihad against the U.S. for its wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said last month that Hasan’s firing squad execution, the first since World War II, would be open to the public and held at Fort Hood. The date of the execution falls on a Thursday, the same day of the week Hasan had planned his attack.

Initial plans to stream Hasan’s execution online were met with a wave of criticism from lawmakers, with Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a retired Navy captain, calling for Hegseth to resign. He argued last month that the Trump administration should be “delivering for the American people,” not “glorifying violence.”

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) compared the announcement to the fall of the Roman Empire, writing on the social platform X, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”

President Trump announced less than a week later that he was canceling the livestream . He said that he heard the criticism, though he suggested that the stream could have deterred terrorists. The president added that “immediate families” of those killed in the shooting could still watch the execution in person.

Three survivors of the shooting who requested the Pentagon to allow them to witness the execution said their requests were denied, ABC News reported .

articles.title: FAA chief to testify on air traffic control overhaul in wake of outages
articles.summary: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford is set to appear before the House Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation next week for a hearing about his agency’s progress on air traffic control system modernization efforts. During the hearing, scheduled for 10 a.m. EST Tuesday, Bedford will discuss the progress of “the Brand-New Air Traffic…
articles.body:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford is set to appear before the House Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation next week for a hearing about his agency’s progress on air traffic control system modernization efforts.

During the hearing, scheduled for 10 a.m. EST Tuesday, Bedford will discuss the progress of “the Brand-New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) initiative and modernizing our nation’s air traffic control system,” according to a press release shared with NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

The announcement comes less than two weeks after the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop , which lasted more than four hours and resulted in the cancellation or delay of thousands of flights. It took days for air travel operations to get back to normal.

Authorities initially said the incident was caused by an overload of data on the routers, blaming old equipment. But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later said a telecommunications line switch led to the stoppage, noting contractor L3Harris had been replacing an older copper wire with a new fiber cable.

Following the incident, Duffy has repeatedly asked Congress for additional funding to update the U.S.’s air traffic control systems, saying, “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

“Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family,” he said. “I want $50 billion.”

In September, Duffy had asked Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country. This came as the FAA began to roll out its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories program, an AI tool designed to help air traffic controllers anticipate congestion and reduce delays.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Duffy’s call for funding to build a new updated system, arguing the technology needs a “complete overhaul.”

Bedford also defended Duffy’s calls for funding, saying, “If we’re going to fix the system, we’re going to return it to the hold standard.”

Duffy is also slated to appear before the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation committee after the Thanksgiving recess. The hearing, scheduled for Dec. 2, will also center on the secretary’s calls to modernize aging air traffic control technology.

articles.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The proposed Character.ai bankruptcy sale includes sensitive personal data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million registered to minors, the state AGs said.
articles.body:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. ( In a blog post , Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”

Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .)

Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

According to federal prosecutors , Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”

But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

articles.summary: Iran is tightening its control over the Strait of Hormuz by increasing its surveillance over the vital waterway, Tehran’s state media reported Wednesday. Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akrami-Nia said the country’s military is on heightened alert and warned vessels that they must coordinate transit with Iranian forces for safe passage, according to Iran’s Tasnim News…
articles.body:
Iran is tightening its control over the Strait of Hormuz by increasing its surveillance over the vital waterway, Tehran’s state media reported Wednesday.

Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akrami-Nia said the country’s military is on heightened alert and warned vessels that they must coordinate transit with Iranian forces for safe passage, according to Iran’s Tasnim News Agency.

Akrami-Nia said Iran’s armed forces had improved their ability to monitor the strait with new systems and by upgrading existing ones, and he accused the U.S. and Israel of having undisclosed objectives in its war against Tehran that went beyond the shuttering the country’s nuclear program.

The warning comes after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Monday three oil tankers escorted through the Strait of Hormuz were hit by underwater mines despite a U.S. military air escort.

“Any transit through unauthorized routes or disregard for communicated warnings constitutes a violation and cooperation with the aggressor forces,” the IRGC said at the time, adding that any alleged violations would be “dealt with firmly in accordance with previously announced regulations.”

And last week, Iran attacked three other tankers in or near the Strait of Hormuz, with two being hit while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait.

The Trump administration’s war against Iran, which began nearly nine months ago, continues with no end in sight as peace talks have failed to move forward.

Since the start of November, the U.S. and Iran have been locked in tit-for-tat strikes , with Tehran targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and American forces most recently attacking Tehran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The activity followed an unofficial quiet period of roughly two months.

The IRGC’s commander in chief, Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, warned on Tuesday that any future fighting between Iran and the U.S. may not be confined to the Middle East and could expand to other locations, if necessary.

To bolster its stance in the region, Washington sent the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier to the Persian Gulf , with the ship last week joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers.

articles.title: Can hackers still read Gmail after a password change?
articles.summary: Remus Stealer malware developers claim Gmail access survives a password change, but Google says the attack targets infected devices, not a Gmail flaw.
articles.body: You change your Gmail password after noticing something suspicious. You sign out of unfamiliar devices and figure your account should be safe again. But what if someone could still read your Gmail after a password change? That's the unsettling claim behind Remus Stealer, a malware service being marketed to cybercriminals. Its developers claim they can keep accessing Gmail messages even after someone resets their password and revokes existing sessions. However, security researchers have not independently verified those claims, and Google disputes the suggestion that the malware exploits a Gmail security flaw. The company says this type of attack targets infected devices rather than Gmail itself. Google also warns that changing your password may not solve the problem if malware remains active on your computer. Here's what the investigation uncovered and how to protect your inbox. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED Hackers claim their malware can keep reading Gmail Security researchers at Hudson Rock examined promotional materials for Remus Stealer, a type of malware designed to collect sensitive information from infected computers. In a November 9 report, the company described a new feature advertised in version 1.3.9 of the malware. The developers claim it allows criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from their control dashboard. The promotional screenshots show lists of emails and individual messages. There's also a "Mail" option connected to records of infected devices. According to the developers, criminals can retrieve email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files. The developers make an even more concerning claim. They say changing a Google password or revoking existing sessions won't necessarily stop someone from accessing the mailbox. They also advertise a way to share mailbox access with other criminals through links. Think about what that could mean if the claims prove true. Someone with access to your Gmail could potentially read private conversations or collect password reset messages for other accounts. However, these claims come from the people selling the malware. Independent researchers have yet to demonstrate that the feature works as advertised. What security researchers actually discovered Hudson Rock contacted the malware developer and spoke with someone who claimed to have used the Gmail feature. That person said they could still access an inbox after closing the browser, resetting a session and changing the Google account password. The developer also described a technique involving browser memory but didn't provide enough technical information to verify it. There are important limits to the investigation. Hudson Rock did not reverse engineer the feature or conduct controlled testing after a complete account recovery. Researchers also couldn't independently verify the customer's claims. Most importantly, the investigation never established that criminals could retrieve newly arriving emails after someone had properly secured their Google account. The screenshots demonstrate that the service advertises a Gmail-reading interface. They don't prove that Remus can defeat Google's protections after a full recovery. There's also no evidence in the report of a previously unknown Gmail security vulnerability. Researchers also could not rule out other explanations, including incomplete session revocation, previously collected messages or unauthorized access that remained active through another route. Without controlled testing, there's no way to confirm exactly how the advertised feature operates. NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH Google responds to the Gmail malware claims We reached out to Google about the research, and the company rejected the suggestion that the reported activity involved a vulnerability in Gmail. A Google spokesperson said: "Attacks involving infostealer malware that target session tokens on personal devices are not new, and there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here. We routinely upgrade our built-in defenses to protect users against session theft and automatically secure accounts when we detect suspicious activity. Users can invalidate stolen sessions by removing malware from the affected device and revoking active sessions via g.co/mydevices." Google explained that this kind of attack targets infected personal devices rather than exploiting Gmail itself. The company also highlighted something especially important for anyone recovering from malware. If the infection remains on a computer when someone resets their password, the malware could capture the new login session. That means a fresh password alone may not solve the problem. Google recommends removing the malware before signing back in on the affected device. From a separate, trusted device, you should also change your password, revoke suspicious sessions through Google's device activity page at myaccount.google.com/device-activity and review your account using Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. The infected computer should remain disconnected until the threat has been removed. The company says it regularly strengthens its defenses against stolen sessions. Those protections include frequent cookie rotation and additional authentication checks when someone attempts sensitive account changes. Google also highlighted Device Bound Session Credentials, a Chrome security technology designed to make stolen session cookies harder to reuse on another device. This protection applies to supported Chrome sessions, with availability depending on the platform and service. These protections help reduce the risk of account theft, although they don't eliminate every possible malware attack. Why hackers may access Gmail without your password You probably open Gmail every day without typing your password. That's because your browser remembers that you've already signed in. Behind the scenes, browsers and applications use session cookies or authentication tokens to maintain access to accounts. These digital credentials help keep you signed in without repeatedly entering your password. Unfortunately, criminals know how valuable that information can be. Infostealer malware can target stored authentication data on an infected computer. If an attacker obtains a valid session, they may be able to access an account without entering the password again. That can also undermine the protection you'd normally expect from two-step verification because the legitimate account holder has already completed the sign-in process. However, a stolen session doesn't automatically give someone unlimited access. Google can invalidate sessions, and some sensitive actions require additional verification. Google's documentation explains that changing a password generally revokes OAuth access and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions, although certain exceptions apply. Google also notes that password changes sign people out of most devices, but some trusted devices and third-party connections may remain signed in. Those exceptions do not prove that Remus uses any of these methods. The concern with an infected computer is that malware may capture fresh authentication information when you sign in again. That's why securing the computer and reviewing account access are essential parts of recovery. Warning signs someone may be accessing your Gmail An unfamiliar Google security alert deserves attention, especially if you haven't signed in from a new device. You should also investigate password reset messages you never requested. These can indicate that someone is attempting to access another account connected to your email address, although an unexpected reset message alone doesn't prove an account has been compromised. Other warning signs include missing messages or people telling you they received strange emails from your address. Check your Sent folder for messages you didn't write. You might also discover forwarding rules or account recovery settings you don't remember changing. If something looks suspicious, open your Google account directly rather than following a link in an unexpected message. Tips to protect your Gmail from malware and hackers If you suspect that someone has accessed your Gmail, take action promptly. The goal is to secure your account while preventing malware from stealing fresh login information. Google emphasizes that removing the infection and revoking compromised sessions are both essential. You can begin securing your account from a trusted device while keeping the suspected infected computer offline. Remove malware from an infected computer If you believe your computer has been infected, disconnect it from the internet. Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing your important accounts. Strong antivirus protection with real-time scanning can help prevent infostealers from gaining access in the first place. However, no antivirus program can guarantee that every threat will be detected. If you suspect that malware stole your login information, change your password promptly and make sure the infected computer cannot capture another session. Do not sign back into Google on the suspected infected computer until you have removed the malware. Google notes that several sessions can appear under the same device name. Review each one and sign out of any you cannot confidently identify. If you've already changed your password while malware was still running, make sure the infected device has been cleaned or remains offline, then change your password again from a trusted device and review active sessions once more. Check for hidden Gmail forwarding rules A criminal who gains access to your Gmail may change settings so incoming messages get forwarded to another email address. That could allow someone to receive copies of new messages even after you change your password. Google requires verification when someone adds a new forwarding address, but you should still check for forwarding that may have been configured without your knowledge. To check your Gmail settings on a computer: Review connected apps and recovery information Some third-party applications can access parts of your Google account after you grant permission. If an unfamiliar app has access to your Gmail, it deserves a closer look. You can also read my CyberGuy guide on apps accessing your Google account for additional instructions. Strengthen your Google account protection Google recommends several protections that can make account takeovers harder. Passkeys offer stronger sign-in security, but they cannot remove an existing infection or automatically prevent theft of an already authenticated session. Google's Advanced Protection Program adds stricter account safeguards, including tighter restrictions on third-party access. Check other accounts connected to your Gmail Remember how many online services use your email address for account recovery. If criminals accessed your mailbox, they may have seen verification messages from other services. Review important accounts for unfamiliar activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected password changes or security alerts. If you reused your Google password anywhere else, change those passwords too. Use unique credentials for every important account, and consider a password manager to keep track of them. For additional protection, my CyberGuy article on identity thieves who don't need your password explains other ways criminals try to get around traditional account security. Kurt's key takeaways For years, changing your password has been one of the first things I've recommended when an online account gets compromised. I still believe that's essential. But this investigation highlights something many people overlook. If malware is running on your computer, it may be able to steal fresh login information after you've changed your password. What concerns me is how much of our digital lives depend on a single Gmail account. Think about the personal messages sitting in your inbox and the accounts that rely on your email for password recovery. Someone who gains access could potentially create problems well beyond your inbox. Google's response makes an important distinction. This is a threat involving malware on infected devices, not a newly demonstrated vulnerability in Gmail. We should also remember that the most alarming claims about this malware have yet to be independently verified. There's a big difference between what criminals advertise and what security researchers can actually demonstrate. articles.title: Trump unveils new tariffs over excess industrial capacity, undeterred by midterms defeat
articles.summary: By David Lawder and Andrea Shalal WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday on 14 major trading partners...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections.

His administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20% to 40% to counter excess industrial capacity that it says these countries are promoting. ‌But the US Trade Representative's office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.

In unveiling the results of an eight-month unfair trade practices investigation ‌into excess industrial capacity, USTR aims to more fully rebuild Trump's tariff leverage after the Supreme Court in February struck down his broad global duties under a national emergencies law.

The effort also seeks to put Trump's tariffs and associated trade agreements on more solid legal and political grounds by backing them ​with a court-tested trade law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and addressing foreign subsidies and industrial policies that are viewed as major trade problems by both Republicans and Democrats.

Separately, USTR proposed a new 10% tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and an increase in duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices.

The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25% tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July under a separate Section 301 investigation. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he decided to propose the tariff increases after months of talks between the US and Brazil made "no meaningful progress."

Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would ‌face the highest capped rate of 20%, which would be added to duties of ⁠roughly 25% imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40%, the USTR said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20% if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35% if negotiations fail.

Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until ⁠after a January 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base.
authors: By David Lawder and Andrea Shalal

articles.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.
articles.body:
Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.
