articles.title: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
articles.summary: 1Password has suffered a data breach impacting customer names and emails. The company says that the incident didn’t impact vaults and the passwords inside them.
articles.body: 1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected. The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers. It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess. The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

articles.title: Fed's Beige Book shows evidence of broadening price pressures
articles.summary: There were "sustained cost pressures" in energy, transportation, healthcare, insurance, and tariff-related expenses.
articles.body:
Anecdotal evidence from across the country this month indicated broader price pressures, bolstering Federal Reserve officials' concerns about persistent inflation.

The Federal Reserve's Beige Book, which compiles anecdotes from businesses and consumers across the country to better understand the economy, shows that during the first two weeks of November there were "sustained cost pressures" in energy, transportation, healthcare, insurance, and tariff-related expenses. Raw materials, metals, freight, and specialized imports also contributed to operating cost pressures. The cost of supplies used to make products generally outpaced increases in selling prices, as competitive pressures and customer price sensitivity limited firms' ability to fully pass through higher costs. The Beige Book noted that businesses expected both expenses and prices to continue rising in the coming months.

The Beige Book was conducted before Wednesday's announcement that the Trump administration is proposing new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the European Union, and 12 other major US trading partners following an eight-month investigation into excess manufacturing capacity.

A fresh reading on the Fed's preferred inflation gauge released Wednesday showed prices heated up more than expected in October . The "core" Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with expectations for 3.2% and up from 3.1% in September. Month over month, core prices held steady at 0.3%, in line with projections.

Meanwhile, the Beige Book showed evidence that the job market is firming, noting that businesses across several sectors cited steady or rising demand for workers but were hesitant to hire due to uncertainty and weakened consumer spending.

The supply of workers generally remained stable, and while it was often relatively easy to find workers, persistent hiring difficulties continued for skilled and technical roles. Overall, employment levels rose slightly, with many firms reporting stable headcounts and hiring primarily to replace attrition, while only a minority reported meaningful increases.

Fed officials will use this on-the-ground information to help make their interest rate decision in two weeks. Markets widely expect the Fed to raise rates for the second time this year by a quarter percentage point.

articles.title: Newly proposed tariffs raise chances of the Fed keeping interest rates higher for longer
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve may have to raise interest rates and keep them higher for longer to combat inflationary pressures
articles.body:
A fresh round of proposed tariffs by the Trump administration raises the likelihood that the Federal Reserve may have to raise interest rates and keep them higher for longer to combat inflationary pressures stemming from the import duties.

The Trump administration proposed new tariffs Wednesday of up to 20% on goods from China, the EU, and 12 other major US trading partners following an eight-month investigation into excess manufacturing capacity.

The proposed 20% tariff on many Chinese goods is described as a "deal rate" that could go higher and be stacked with preexisting tariffs, resulting in a total rate over 40% on some Chinese goods.

Greg Daco, chief economist at EY, thinks the new tariffs raise the risk of "a more hawkish Fed response" given that inflation is at a three-year high.

"The concern is that tariffs add another supply-side cost shock at a time when demand remains resilient enough for businesses to pass a larger share of those costs through to consumers," Daco told Yahoo Finance.

He thinks more policymakers may favor raising rates earlier as evidence of inflation persistence builds rather than waiting for those pressures to become embedded and potentially require more rate hikes later.

Many members of the Fed, including New York Fed president John Williams, have been sanguine that tariffs were largely washing out of the inflation picture. But he warned this week that the outlook for inflation could change if new tariffs were put in place.

"The encouraging news is that the effects of tariffs on inflation have largely abated and should not add significantly to inflation in goods prices in the future," Williams said in a speech on Monday. "Of course, this could change if new tariffs were introduced."

Put plainly, new tariffs raise the prospect of further rate hikes and holding rates higher for longer.

The Fed is widely expected to raise rates next month by a quarter percentage point, with markets already expecting at least one more rate hike in the first quarter given the current inflation landscape.

The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heated up more than expected in October . The "core" Personal Consumption Expenditures index, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with expectations for 3.2% and up from 3.1% in September. Month over month, core prices held steady at 0.3%, in line with projections.

articles.title: US airlines face higher costs from proposed Embraer duty
articles.summary: By Allison Lampert and Gabriel Araujo Nov 25 (Reuters) - A proposed 10% US duty on finished Embraer aircraft from Brazil would raise costs for US airlines th...
articles.body:
Nov 25 (Reuters) - A proposed 10% US duty on finished Embraer aircraft from Brazil would raise costs for US airlines that have no US-made alternatives, analysts and executives said on ‌Wednesday, as the Trump administration uses the jet market as trade leverage.

Aerospace, a major export sector for the ‌United States, has largely escaped US President Donald Trump's tariffs that have hit other industries like autos, steel and aluminum.

The Trump administration floated the unexpected duties ​on commercial jets and other goods from Brazil as part of a broader round of tariffs proposed on goods from more than a dozen trading partners.

Trump previously reversed course on a call to ban Canadian-made Bombardier private jets from the US after it emerged that some aircraft were being completed in Wichita, Kansas, for military contracts.

Imposing the tariffs, which could come as early as January, ‌would raise the price US carriers pay ⁠for Embraer jets at a time when they are already grappling with a surge in jet fuel prices due to the Iran war.

As of the end of the third quarter, Embraer had ⁠a firm order backlog of around 160 E175 jets combined for US carriers American Airlines, SkyWest Airlines and Republic Airways, according to company filings.

American Airlines expects five deliveries of Embraer commercial jets for its American Eagle regional feeder carriers by year's end and another 14 ​in 2027, ​according to company filings. The airline referred a request for comment ​to airline trade group Airlines for America, which ‌was not immediately available.

"There is no US competitor to Embraer jetliners," said Richard Aboulafia, managing director at Michigan-based AeroDynamic Advisory.

Aboulafia said he did not believe the Trump administration would follow through with the threats on Embraer, in part due to pressure from a Democratic-led US House and Senate in January and because the company has factories in Republican-leaning Florida.

"This is every bit as big a threat to Embraer jets as tariff threats were to Bombardier jets," Aboulafia said. "In other words, it will not ‌happen."

Embraer said it strongly defends the zero-tariff regime for global aerospace. It ​also said it has $3.5 billion in assets and more than 2,500 employees ​across the US.

Analysts were divided over the impact the ​tariffs would have on Embraer's Praetor executive jet, which is flown as an unfinished, or "green," aircraft, ‌without paint or interiors to the company's Florida factory ​where it is completed.

articles.title: Analysis-For Trump, doubling down on tariffs is about power, not popularity
articles.summary: By Trevor Hunnicutt and Andrea Shalal PALM BEACH, Florida, Nov 25 (Reuters) - In midterm elections three weeks ago, US voters punished Republicans over an ec...
articles.body:
PALM BEACH, Florida, Nov 25 (Reuters) - In midterm elections three weeks ago, US voters punished Republicans over an economy and inflation that many said were made worse by tariffs. President Donald Trump is doubling down on them anyway.

The Trump administration on Wednesday announced a new round of tariffs on goods from 14 major trading ‌partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, a seemingly counterintuitive move that reflects both Trump's decades-old belief in tariffs and a new political reality confronting his White House.

With Democrats set to ‌control Congress for the final two years of his presidency, tariffs are taking on added importance as one of the most potent economic tools Trump can wield without lawmakers' approval.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imports, raising costs for consumers. But Trump sees them ​as a way to wring concessions from foreign leaders, force corporate CEOs to build plants in the US, raise cash for the government and curry favor with blue-collar voters, according to US officials and other people familiar with the president's thinking.

And after a midterm defeat for his party that threatens to sharply constrain his domestic agenda, Trump is eager to demonstrate that he remains capable of driving economic policy and exercising power even as his legislative clout diminishes, the people said.

"This is all because of tariffs," Trump told CNBC on Monday as he touted new factories being built in the US. But he said the policy could come with costs. "There's going to be ‌always that little headache during this little transition period."

Some Republicans in Congress ⁠were quick to blame the president's tariff policy for the party's stunning midterm losses. Two-thirds of voters said Trump's tariff policies hurt the national economy, compared with 21% who said they had helped and 12% who found no difference, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets. ⁠Yale University's Budget Lab estimated earlier this month that tariffs raised US household costs by $900 annually.

The administration nevertheless proposed new tariffs that would increase duties on targeted imports, with maximum rates of 20% to 40%, though completed or pending trade deals would generally limit them to 10% to 20%.

The new policy, which followed an eight-month review of trading partners' practices, revamps a set of tariffs that Trump imposed in 2025 and the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in ​February.
authors: By Trevor Hunnicutt and Andrea Shalal

articles.title: Amazon loses its latest attempt to get out of handling more recall notices
articles.summary: A court ruled in favor of the US CPSC’s argument that Amazon is responsible for recalled products that other companies sell on its platforms.
articles.body: Amazon is on the hook to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after losing its legal battle against the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The US District Court for the District of Maryland ruled in favor of the CPSC, which argued that Amazon is a distributor of goods, not a logistics provider, making it responsible for carrying out recalls of third-party products. Amazon sued the CPSC in March 2025 after the agency ordered Amazon to recall over 400,000 “Fulfilled by Amazon” products that pose a “substantial product hazard,” including faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers without electrocution protection, and children’s sleepwear that doesn’t meet federal flammability standards. As a result, Amazon will be required to implement the following measures, initially outlined in the CPSC’s January 2025 order: > Notification: > On the day CPSC publishes the recall releases, Amazon must notify the public by posting the recall releases to Amazon.com; notify original purchasers directly via email and by providing information regarding the recalls on each purchaser’s “Your Orders” page. > Amazon must provide one round of notice of the recalls to Fulfilled by Amazon participants that sold the subject products. > Incentive to Remove Products from Commerce: > Amazon must issue a full refund in the amount of the purchase price to any consumer who submits proof of destruction or disposal of a subject product. > Maintaining Records of Recalls: > Amazon must maintain the recall releases on the “Recalls and Product Safety Alerts” webpage on amazon.com for a minimum of five years. > Amazon must submit monthly progress reports for five years and maintain records of its actions to comply with the Order for the same period. “We have a longstanding commitment to removing unsafe and recalled products from our store and notifying customers, backed by an industry-leading recalls process,” Amazon spokesperson Sammy Brill says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “We’re reviewing our options following the ruling and look forward to continuing to work with the CPSC to put customer safety first.” Update, November 25th: Added Amazon’s statement.

articles.title: US Partners Respond to Tariffs With Anger, Protest and Diplomacy
articles.summary: Major US trading partners responded with disappointment and protests while holding out the prospect of negotiations after the Trump administration rolled out...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Major US trading partners responded with disappointment and protests while holding out the prospect of negotiations after the Trump administration rolled out a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies.

For now, officials from Singapore to Japan are signaling a preference for negotiation over retaliation, even as China and the European Union have made clear they could hit back if Washington pushes beyond the terms of existing trade deals. The Trump administration plans to impose levies on imports from economies it accuses of contributing to excess manufacturing capacity and hurting US companies.

The new tariffs mark the latest effort by the Trump administration to reinstate an expansive trade agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by the Supreme Court in February, forcing the president to invoke other legal authorities to restore the duties.

Singapore said it disagreed with the US findings that its policies contribute to a glut in manufacturing capacity and will urge Washington to reconsider proposed tariffs of up to 20% on the city-state's exports.

The rate could be lowered to 10% if Singapore reaches a reciprocal trade agreement with the US or concludes other negotiations that address Washington's concerns.

"Singapore's economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidize manufacturing for export," the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said Thursday. "Our free trade agreements seek to lower barriers to trade and investments."

Japan protested US plans to impose a 15% levy on its products, with the chief government spokesman calling the move "regrettable."

"Japan does not have any non-market policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a regular news conference.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters at a briefing Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was "political maneuvering" and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce.

For many economies, the proposed rates are broadly in line with levels previously negotiated with Washington before the court's decision. They aren't expected to take effect until after a written-comment period and public hearings, with implementation possible in late January.

articles.title: 42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
articles.summary: A bipartisan coalition of 42 state attorneys general say Character.AI is planning to sell the personal data of minors to the highest bidder.
articles.body: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.” In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs. The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed. Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

articles.title: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries
articles.summary: "On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18bn to the deficit by 2034," Oxford Economics notes.
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump's term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line. Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark's national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics' Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s "are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade."

Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes.

"On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO's estimate," Zwemmer wrote

From a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer says that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration.

articles.title: FedEx plane overruns Miami runway, snarling Thanksgiving travel
articles.summary: A FedEx cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport late Wednesday, triggering widespread flight delays during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. The airport said in a statement that the incident occurred around 8:40 p.m., forcing the temporary closure of all but its south runway. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews responded,…
articles.body:
A FedEx cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport late Wednesday, triggering widespread flight delays during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

The airport said in a statement that the incident occurred around 8:40 p.m., forcing the temporary closure of all but its south runway. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue crews responded, and no injuries were reported.

Airport officials urged passengers to check with their airlines for updated flight information before heading to the airport.

“We appreciate our passengers’ patience as we work to safely resume normal operations,” the officials said.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which is investigating the incident , reported hourslong flight delays early Thursday.

FedEx confirmed Flight 910 from Memphis, Tenn., experienced “an issue upon landing” Wednesday evening.

“We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries,” the company said in a statement. “We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA.”

As of early Thursday, 34 flights into or out of Miami International Airport had been canceled and six others had been delayed, according to FlightAware data .

The incident follows a string of aviation mishaps at the Miami airport, including a September crash involving an Amazon cargo plane that killed five people on the ground.

The Trump administration has been ramping up its push to overhaul the nation’s aging air traffic control system. That effort was exacerbated after a router malfunction triggered a nationwide ground stop earlier this month.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has since asked Congress for an additional $50.1 billion to modernize the system , on top of the $12.5 billion lawmakers approved last year as part of President Trump’s sweeping tax and spending package.

Inclement weather and higher airfare tied to rising fuel costs amid the Iran war have also complicated Thanksgiving travel for millions of Americans.

articles.title: Trump rips Obama, CNN as he touts ‘perfect’ Iowa detonation
articles.summary: President Trump took swipes at former President Obama and CNN over what he described as his administration’s “perfect” detonation of degraded lead azide in Iowa — a controversial move that’s raised questions around how the explosive material accumulated to that degree in the first place. In a post on Truth Social early Thursday, Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump took swipes at former President Obama and CNN over what he described as his administration’s “perfect” detonation of degraded lead azide in Iowa — a controversial move that’s raised questions around how the explosive material accumulated to that degree in the first place.

In a post on Truth Social early Thursday, Trump wrote that “0.000% of Obama caused carcinogens were released into beautiful Iowa air after the Perfect detonation.”

Trump, in a separate post , called CNN’s coverage ahead of the planned Iowa lead detonation “inaccurate and deplorable” and asserted without explanation “They want our Country to lose.”

The U.S. Army detonated the deteriorated lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday, with the government saying the move was justified to avoid a potential explosion. Following the blast, Trump administration officials and Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle touted the operation as a “huge success.”

Residents in Middletown, Iowa, were recommended to evacuate the area before the planned detonation. A shelter-in-place order was later lifted.

However, the planned explosion sparked concerns around possible health and environmental impacts, given that lead is a toxic material that can pose serious health risks including brain and nervous system damage and anemia for babies and young children, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. It can also cause heart-related problems and decreased kidney function in adults.

Both Trump and Vice President Vance have sought to put the blame on Obama for the Hawkeye State’s buildup of the toxic lead azide, suggesting it dated back to 2009. However, critics have raised questions around why the administration didn’t tackle the issue during the president’s first term.

Trump has often attacked media outlets like CNN and MS NOW over its coverage of the White House. A federal judge has also blocked efforts by the administration to bar Politico, MS NOW and CNN from going to the White House.

The Hill has reached out to CNN and Obama’s office for comment.

articles.title: Your holiday shopping data needs a cleanup before Black Friday
articles.summary: Data brokers may expose your name, home address and phone number to scammers sending fake USPS delivery texts ahead of the Black Friday shopping rush.
articles.body: Your phone buzzes: "USPS: Your package could not be delivered due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours." You did order something last week. Probably several things. So your thumb hovers over the link. That's the whole trick. Black Friday lands on Nov. 27 this year, and the holiday delivery rush is already underway. That gives scammers plenty of opportunities to send fake delivery alerts that arrive when you're expecting a package. Meanwhile, your shopping habits and personal details may be circulating through data brokers. Here's how that information can make scams more convincing and what you can do to clean it up before the holiday shopping rush gets even busier. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? How your holiday shopping profile gets built Every time you shop online, sign up for a discount or share your contact information, you may add to a growing collection of personal data. Some businesses use that information for their own marketing, while others share certain details with advertising partners or data brokers. Here's where some of that information comes from: As I've covered before, loyalty programs and store memberships can contribute to the information companies collect about you. Add the personal details available through people-search sites, and someone looking to target you may find more information than you'd expect. The FTC explains that people-search companies collect information from multiple sources and sell reports containing personal details, sometimes including relatives' names and addresses. You can use the free exposure scanner we recommend at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. Keep in mind that a free scan cannot uncover every private data broker database. The results might surprise you. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES How scammers turn personal information into a delivery scam A fake delivery text doesn't need to know exactly what you ordered. During the holidays, plenty of people are expecting packages, so a message about a delivery problem can seem believable. Scammers often send these messages to large numbers of phone numbers without knowing anything about the recipients. However, personal information obtained from public sources or data brokers can help make some scams more convincing. Here's how that information could be misused: The FTC reported that fake package delivery problems, often involving messages impersonating USPS, were the most commonly reported type of text scam in 2024. The problem extends beyond package deliveries. According to FTC testimony released in March 2026, Americans reported $15.9 billion in fraud losses during 2025 across all scam categories. A typical fake delivery message directs you to a convincing website and asks you to pay a small redelivery fee. That payment request is the trap. The scammer wants your credit card details and may also try to collect other sensitive information. Here's something important to remember: USPS does not charge a fee for redelivery. Its legitimate text tracking service also requires you to request tracking information first, and those tracking messages do not contain links. Why the cleanup should happen before Black Friday Data removal takes time. Brokers process opt-out requests on different schedules, and personal information can reappear even after it has been removed. Starting now gives you a chance to identify exposed information and begin requesting removals before the busiest shopping days arrive. There is one important distinction. Removing your information from data brokers can reduce your exposure over time, but it cannot guarantee that scam texts will stop or prevent scammers from contacting you this holiday season. That's why data cleanup should go hand in hand with safer shopping and delivery habits. Your 15-minute pre-Black Friday cleanup You can get started in about 15 minutes, although completing data removal requests and having companies process them can take much longer. 1. Search for yourself first Look up your name on people-search websites such as Spokeo, Whitepages or BeenVerified. Check whether your home address, phone number or relatives' information appears. If you find information you want removed, look for the site's opt-out instructions. 2. Review your shopping accounts Check the privacy settings on the websites and apps you use most frequently. Look for options to limit promotional emails, personalized advertising and sharing with marketing partners. You can also review saved shipping addresses and remove outdated entries you no longer need. Keep in mind that deleting a saved address may not erase information retained in previous order records. 3. Track orders in the app, never through an unexpected text link If a message claims there's a delivery problem, open the retailer's or shipping company's official app or website yourself. Check the tracking number and delivery status there. Do not enter payment details through a link in an unsolicited message, even if it includes your name or address. 4. Use an automated data removal service Instead of spending hours submitting individual opt-out forms, an automated data removal service can send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, depending on the provider and plan you choose. Some services also submit recurring removal requests to help address information that reappears. While no service can erase every piece of information about you online, it can help reduce your exposure. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 5. Set a family rule about delivery texts Talk with your parents and other relatives about fake delivery messages. Make sure everyone knows to verify unexpected payment requests through the carrier's official website or app. For USPS specifically, explain that it does not charge redelivery fees. A message demanding immediate payment to release a package should raise suspicion. 6. Report suspicious texts If you receive a suspicious delivery message, don't respond or click the link. You can forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and use your phone's reporting feature. For messages impersonating USPS, you can also report them to spam@uspis.gov. If you already entered your credit card information on a suspicious website, contact your card issuer immediately. Ask about blocking the card, disputing fraudulent charges and monitoring your account for unauthorized activity. You can also report the incident at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most about these fake delivery texts is how easily they blend into our holiday routines. When you're ordering gifts and waiting for packages, a message about a delivery problem can catch you at exactly the wrong moment. I also think we need to pay more attention to how much personal information is floating around online. Taking a few minutes to search your name, review your shopping accounts and start removing exposed information is worthwhile. But remember, even if you clean up your data, scammers can still reach you. My advice is simple: Never let an unexpected text dictate how you check on a package. Open the official app or website yourself and verify what's actually happening before you share a single detail. Have you received a fake package delivery text that looked convincing, and how did you figure out it was a scam? articles.body:
Severe storms and flooding on both the Pacific Northwest and East Coasts are wreaking havoc on Thanksgiving travel and festivities this week.

The National Weather Service (NWS) noted in a short-range forecast discussion published Thursday that low pressure moving upward from the southeast would bring heavy rain on New England — including potential flash flooding and isolated thunderstorms in the southeast into the end of the weekend.

Both New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) declared states of emergency amid the fierce weather .

Rainfall and some higher-elevation snow were also predicted for parts of the Pacific Northwest, according to the NWS.

The flight-tracking site FlightAware showed that 500 flights into, within and out of the U.S. were delayed in addition to 365 flights that were cancelled. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy signaled earlier this week that most of the delays are tied to weather, though recent system outages across airlines have also drawn scrutiny.

Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport, Miami International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport reported the highest numbers of delayed or cancelled flights throughout the country as of Thursday morning.

The storms posed such a threat in New York that Macy’s announced on Wednesday that their annual Thanksgiving Day Parade would be pushed back to Saturday.

Meanwhile, king tides — some spanning as high as over 8 feet, according to The New York Times — have swept through states like California and Oregon, prompting the partial collapse of a pier and serious flooding .

A coastal flood warning is also in effect, according to National Weather Service Portland, and is expected to run through Friday.

Denny’s, the popular breakfast spot, celebrated Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO on Wednesday, highlighting its decades-long ties to the embattled tech executive .

The diner chain said it restored a plaque marking the booth at its San Jose, Calif., restaurant where Jensen Huang and his co-founders came up with the idea for the chipmaking giant in 1993. He also previously worked as a dishwasher and server for the restaurant.

“Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” Denny’s wrote in a statement shared to social platform X on Wednesday.

“We put the plaque right back up where it belongs,” Denny’s said, noting that Jensen Huang has referred to the diner chain as his first alma mater.

“Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee’s on. We’re always open, 24/7,” the diner added.

The Justice and Commerce departments have confirmed they are looking into Megaspeed , a Singaporean firm tied to Nvidia that is suspected of funneling chips to China. Alice Huang, who was in contact with Chinese intelligence and had an affair with the tech executive, previously worked at the firm.

Blanche faced a barrage of questions from reporters earlier this week about the government’s probes but stopped short of clarifying whether Jensen Huang himself had been investigated.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have raised concerns about Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia and the Trump administration’s role in securing his reinstatement.

articles.title: Federal judge blocks the FCC from reviewing ABC’s licenses early
articles.summary: The FCC has been prohibited from taking further action in the early review of ABC’s licenses, and its efforts to dismiss the network’s lawsuit were rejected.
articles.body: US District Judge Loren AliKhan has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses in a preliminary injunction, and rejected its efforts to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of violating its free speech rights and claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast. In her ruling the judge noted that the network was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.” Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump. In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest. ”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

articles.title: Housefishing could fool you with AI real estate photos
articles.summary: Housefishing scams use AI real estate photos to fool buyers. Google Lens reverse image search and live video walkthroughs can help expose the fakes.
articles.body: You find a beautiful house online. The driveway looks brand new, and the landscaping could be straight out of a home magazine. You get excited, schedule a showing and start thinking about where your furniture might go. Then you pull up to the address and wonder whether you're looking at the same house. That's the growing concern behind housefishing, a term for real estate listings that use digitally altered or AI-generated photos to make properties look better than they actually are. A recent report highlighted complaints from homebuyers and renters who described misleading property pictures as "false advertising." With AI tools becoming more convincing, it's getting harder to know whether you're looking at a home's actual condition or a digital makeover. So how can you tell whether a listing photo shows the home you're actually getting, and what should you check before scheduling a tour? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. HIS HOME CHANGED HANDS FOR $5. COULD IT HAPPEN TO YOUR FAMILY? What is housefishing in real estate? Housefishing happens when property photos create an unrealistic impression of a home. AI can make an outdated property appear freshly renovated without anyone doing the actual work. For instance, two photos can show the same two-story house, but create very different impressions. The original photo can show a home with a dark asphalt driveway and large shrubs covering much of the front porch. But an AI-enhanced version can show a clean concrete driveway and a newly styled entrance. This example shows how digital alterations can make a property appear to have undergone an expensive makeover. If those improvements exist only in the edited photo, someone visiting the property could be in for an unpleasant surprise. When do AI real estate photos become misleading? Virtual staging has been around for years. Adding digital furniture to an empty living room can help buyers understand how they might use the space. AI simply makes those transformations easier and more realistic. But replacing a worn-out kitchen with an AI-generated renovation is another story. Laurent Cardinal, founder of real estate technology company Planpoint at planpoint.io/, believes agents need to be upfront about what they've changed. "The line is drawn where the intent is," Cardinal explains. He supports using AI to show what a home could look like after renovations, provided agents clearly disclose the changes. His recommendation is straightforward: Show the original photo alongside the edited version so prospective buyers can compare them. However, digitally hiding property defects or replacing an unattractive view crosses that line. "That's cheating and it's hurtful to everyone in the market," Cardinal says. A misleading listing can waste someone's time and influence important financial decisions. For renters, the consequences can be especially serious if they send a deposit based on photos that fail to reflect the property. Why AI-generated property photos are getting harder to spot You might think you'd recognize an AI-generated photo immediately. Maybe the furniture looks strange or a window seems out of place. Unfortunately, today's tools can produce convincing results. Sometimes the changes are subtle enough to escape a close look. Cardinal warns that even people familiar with AI-generated content can struggle to identify it. "But there's no silver bullet here, and anyone can get caught," he says. Unusually perfect rooms can raise questions, especially when architectural details appear inconsistent between photos. However, traditional real estate photography can also be misleading. Wide-angle lenses make rooms appear larger, while carefully chosen lighting can minimize visible imperfections. AI creates an additional concern because it can alter the features of the property itself. That makes it increasingly difficult to judge a home's condition from listing photos alone. FAKE VACATION RENTAL SITES USE LIVE CHAT TO STEAL YOUR DATA Are agents required to disclose AI-altered real estate photos? The rules depend on where the property is located and which listing service an agent uses. California has already taken action. Under Assembly Bill 723, which took effect Jan. 1, 2026, real estate professionals must disclose covered digital alterations in advertisements for properties for sale. They must also provide access to the original, unaltered photos. The law covers changes made using traditional editing software or AI. Routine adjustments to lighting or color generally fall outside the requirements when they don't misrepresent the property. California has also approved Assembly Bill 2025. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the state will require disclosures for digitally altered rental advertisements, with access to original photos when existing pictures have been changed. Meanwhile, New York has warned agents about misleading AI property pictures. In November 2025, the New York Department of State reminded real estate professionals that advertisements must accurately represent properties for sale or rent. Agents who publish deceptive advertisements can face disciplinary action. Multiple listing services have their own restrictions. Stellar MLS, for example, requires disclosure of virtually staged photos and prohibits edits that conceal property defects or alter permanent features. There is currently no single nationwide law requiring every AI-edited real estate photo to carry a disclosure. Still, existing advertising laws and professional rules can apply when pictures mislead prospective buyers. Can AI help detect housefishing? Interestingly, the same technology creating misleading property photos may also help identify them. Cardinal's company, Planpoint, connects listing photos to interactive floor plans. That allows prospective buyers to see how rooms fit together instead of relying on individual pictures that may be difficult to interpret. Its Planpoint Visit platform also offers AI photo detection. The technology checks newly uploaded property photos for signs of AI generation and displays a warning when it finds something suspicious. Cardinal says the company achieved a 98% success rate in its internal testing. How to protect yourself from housefishing Before scheduling a showing or putting money down on a property, there are several ways to check whether the listing photos tell the whole story. Ask for the original, unedited photos If a home looks suspiciously polished, ask the agent whether any pictures have been digitally altered. Request the original photos so you can compare them. Pay particular attention to kitchens and bathrooms, where expensive renovations can significantly affect a home's value. If an agent cannot explain what was changed, ask more questions before moving forward. Request a live video walkthrough Cardinal recommends a simple way to verify a property's appearance. "The easiest way is to request a live video call with the agent or the owner," he says. Ask to see the areas you're most interested in, including anything that looks unusually perfect in the listing. A live walkthrough can reveal details that edited photos might hide. However, it cannot prove that the person showing the home has authority to rent or sell it. Compare the listing photos with the floor plan Look carefully at the room dimensions and window locations. Then compare those details with the photos. Cardinal suggests asking, "Do the rooms and angles add up?" If a small bedroom appears enormous in a listing, ask whether the pictures were digitally altered. Remember that wide-angle photography can also exaggerate the apparent size of a room. Check the house on Google Street View Search the property's address in Google Maps and look at the exterior using Street View. Compare the driveway and surrounding homes with what's shown in the listing. You might notice changes that deserve a closer look. However, Street View pictures can be outdated, so differences don't automatically mean an agent used AI. Reverse-search the property photos Use Google Lens or another reverse-image search tool to check whether the same property pictures appear elsewhere online. You may find older listings showing the home before it was digitally enhanced. You could also discover that someone copied photos from another property to create a fraudulent rental advertisement. For help getting started, see our guide on how to reverse search an image on your phone. Verify the property before sending money Never rely solely on listing photos when making a financial commitment. If you're renting, independently verify the identity and authority of the landlord or agent before sending a deposit. For a home purchase, arrange an in-person showing and an independent inspection before committing to buy. A polished listing photo cannot tell you whether the property has hidden problems. Kurt's key takeaways Those example of the two photos of the same house really show how far AI has come. The updated version looks fantastic, and I can see why someone would want to schedule a showing. But what happens when you arrive and discover that the beautiful driveway and landscaping don't actually exist? I think AI can be a great tool for helping buyers see a home's potential, especially if they're considering renovations. The problem starts when agents present those digital upgrades as the real thing. Buying a home is a major investment, and people deserve to know exactly what they're getting before they fall in love with a property online. I'd like to see more transparency from real estate agents, with original photos available alongside any AI-enhanced versions. There's nothing wrong with showing what a house could become, but buyers should never have to guess what it looks like today. Would you walk away from a home if you discovered the agent had used AI to make it look better than it actually was, or would you consider that acceptable marketing? articles.title: FIFA: ‘Limited set of personal and business information’ stolen in cyber attack
articles.summary: FIFA, the international governing body for soccer, said Thursday that it had been subject to a cyberattack that resulted in a “limited set of personal and business information” that was stolen. “FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyber-attack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and…
articles.body:
FIFA, the international governing body for soccer, said Thursday that it had been subject to a cyberattack that resulted in a “limited set of personal and business information” that was stolen.

“FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyber-attack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” the governing body said in a statement to The Hill, adding that it’s convening the appropriate officials to investigate the incident.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” FIFA said. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

Sources who spoke with The Athletic said the cyberattack happened as a result of the hacker or hackers pretending to be staff of the football governing body. A group called the Handsome Boy Hacking Club has claimed to be behind the cyberattack, according to various news outlets, though FIFA did not identify who was behind the move.

Less than a tenth of a percent of the body’s data was compromised, those sources told The Athletic. BBC reported that a sell-off plan pitched by FIFA President Gianni Infantino, which has since been ditched, was not a part of the data compromised.

The FBI warned in May that cyber actors were trying to create websites that looked akin to the international soccer governing body’s online domain to collect personal information and sell fake soccer tickets.

“Spoofed websites may mimic the legitimate URL by using a minor misspelling, such as fiffa[.]com, or alternative top-level domains, such as .org rather than .com,” the FBI said in an advisory earlier this year. “This form of cyberattack — called typo squatting — relies on Internet users making mistakes, such as common typos, when visiting a URL. Threat actors may also register illegitimate websites such as jobs-fifa[.]com to impersonate legitimate subdomains.”

“If a threat actor gains access to a victim’s [personal identifiable information], they can create new accounts in a victim’s name and ultimately defraud the victim,” the FBI added.

articles.title: Zeldin: No airborne lead detected in Iowa a day after Army blast
articles.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors have detected no airborne lead following the Army’s controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa, though the agency is still awaiting laboratory results from its environmental testing. Lee Zeldin, administrator of the EPA, said more than 300 agency employees…
articles.body:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors have detected no airborne lead following the Army’s controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa, though the agency is still awaiting laboratory results from its environmental testing.

Lee Zeldin, administrator of the EPA, said more than 300 agency employees and contractors have collected more than 1,000 samples of air, soil and water since Wednesday’s detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

“EPA’s 4 Xact air monitors have all reported a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead since the mitigated detonation,” Zeldin wrote on social media Thursday morning.

The agency expects to complete sample collection by the end of Thursday and begin receiving laboratory results as early as Friday.

Vice President Vance praised the agency’s efforts Thursday on social media following Zeldin’s update.

“Amazing job to Lee and the team at EPA. Proud of our team,” Vance wrote on social media Thursday afternoon.

President Trump similarly touted the initial reports from Iowa on Wednesday, saying the Army’s mitigation efforts had “far exceeded expectations.”

The federal government has maintained that the detonation was necessary to prevent an uncontrolled explosion involving the deteriorating material, which the Army deemed too dangerous to transport. The operation drew scrutiny from residents, public health experts and lawmakers concerned about the potential contamination of surrounding communities and farmland.

In children, exposure to the toxic metal can cause brain damage, nervous system damage, anemia, learning problems and behavioral issues, according to the EPA.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) ripped the Trump administration over the detonation after accusing officials of failing to adequately address the health risks of detonating 5 tons of lead munitions.

“The potential fallout could span multiple states and has forced Americans to evacuate their homes the day before Thanksgiving,” Jeffries said Wednesday in a statement.

Federal officials lifted a shelter-in-place order Wednesday evening after declaring the operation a success. In a joint statement, six federal agencies said the detonation successfully eliminated the threat posed by the deteriorating lead azide and said Iowa residents in the affected area could safely resume their normal activities.

Augusta lies along the perimeter of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, where earlier that day the U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of lead azide.

articles.title: Musk pledges 2 SpaceX shares per American child
articles.summary: SpaceX and its CEO Elon Musk announced Wednesday that they would each donate a share of the aerospace company’s stock to every American child with an active “Trump Account” — doubling a pledge the billionaire made last month. The company said in a statement it would issue new shares of its Class A common stock…
articles.body:
SpaceX and its CEO Elon Musk announced Wednesday that they would each donate a share of the aerospace company’s stock to every American child with an active “Trump Account” — doubling a pledge the billionaire made last month.

The company said in a statement it would issue new shares of its Class A common stock to those with active Trump Accounts, an investment account for American children that helps build long-term savings. Musk also intends on personally matching the stocks donated by SpaceX.

“SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary,” the company said. “We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit.”

Musk wrote Thursday on social platform X that SpaceX would distribute its shares next month.

“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he added.

Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX’s president and chief operating officer, previously pledged to donate more than 2 million shares of the company’s stock through the program. The gift will go to children from low-income areas between the ages of 11 and 17, primarily focusing on those who live near her home in central Texas.

The announcement comes after the Treasury Department said Tuesday that friends and family members had contributed more than $1 billion to individual Trump Accounts, bringing the total deposits in President Trump’s child investment program to more than $9 billion.

Nearly 70 million accounts have been established under the program, including more than 60 million through the administration’s automatic enrollment initiative announced in October.

The tax-advantaged investment accounts were established under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025. Children younger than 18 with valid Social Security numbers are eligible for accounts. Those born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 — the duration of Trump’s second term in office — qualify for a one-time $1,000 contribution from the federal government.

The program has attracted billions of dollars in philanthropic commitments, including a $6.25 billion pledge from Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell, to provide $250 to children living in ZIP codes with a median family income of $150,000 or less.

articles.title: Thanksgiving storms ground DC flights, knock out power for more than 850K
articles.summary: A powerful coastal storm disrupted Thanksgiving travel in the Washington, D.C., area on Thursday as heavy rain and winds stopped flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA). Along the East Coast, hundreds and thousands of homes and businesses lost power, along with more in the Midwest. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground…
articles.body:
A powerful coastal storm disrupted Thanksgiving travel in the Washington, D.C., area on Thursday as heavy rain and winds stopped flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

Along the East Coast, hundreds and thousands of homes and businesses lost power, along with more in the Midwest.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop temporarily at DCA due to thunderstorms.

The agency also warned of potential ground stops at Washington Dulles International Airport and Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport in Maryland through the evening.

More than 420 flights had been canceled nationwide and nearly 2,000 flights were delayed by late Thursday afternoon, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware , with airports serving Washington and New York City among the hardest hit.

Most major airlines have issued travel waivers for the affected Thanksgiving flights, including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and JetBlue.

Meanwhile, more than 850,000 utility customers were without electricity nationwide as of 5 p.m. EST, according to PowerOutage.us , with Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania accounting for more than half of the outages.

More than 178,000 customers in Virginia and 174,000 in Maryland were without power, while Pennsylvania recorded roughly 154,000 outages. Another 86,000 customers in New Jersey and nearly 20,000 in Delaware faced electricity outages.

Water customers in the Maryland suburbs of D.C. were asked by Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission to conserve water in the face of power outages at filtration plants at midafternoon Thursday.

The National Weather Service reported wind gusts of between 50 and 70 mph across portions of the East Coast including Virginia, Maryland, New York and coastal New England.

The threat of severe weather prompted officials to postpone the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, making the first weather-related postponement in the event’s history.

The parade is now scheduled to take place at 8:30 a.m. EST on Saturday, which New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will miss because he is scheduled to have surgery Friday on his right leg after tearing his Achilles tendon .
